args.text:
CHICAGO, May 4, 189-

_Dear Pierrepont:_ The cashier's just handed me your expense account for the month, and it fair makes a bloke hunch his shoulders to look it over. When I told you I wanted you to get a liberal education, I didn't mean I wanted to buy Cambridge. Course the bills won't break me, but they'll break you unless you're dead careful, son.

I've noticed for the last two years that your accounts have been getting heavier every month, but I haven't seen any sign of you taking honours to justify the extra running costs; and that's bad business, a good deal like feeding his weight in corn to a mongrel steer that won't fatten up.

I haven't said anything about this before, cos I trusted a fair bit to your native common sense to keep you from making a mug of yourself the way some of these young blokes who've never had to work for it do. But just because I've sat tight, don't go getting it into your head that the old man's loaded and can stand it, cos he won't stand it once you leave uni. The sooner you fit your spending to what your earning will be, the easier the two of them will find it to live together.

The only sure way a bloke can get rich quick is to have it handed to him or to inherit it. You're not going to get rich that way, not until you've proved you can hold down a pretty important job with the firm, anyway; and of course there's only one place a bloke can start from for that job at Graham & Co. Doesn't matter a scrap whether he's the son of the old man or of the cellar boss: that place is the bottom. And the bottom in the office end of this business is a seat at the mailing-desk, with eight quid every Saturday night.

I can't hand you any ready-made success. It'd do you no good, and it'd do the house harm. There's plenty of room at the top here, but there's no lift in the building. Starting, like you are, with a good education, you ought to climb quicker than the bloke who hasn't got one; but there'll come a time, when you start at the factory, when you won't lick stamps as fast as the other young fellas at the desk. Yet the bloke who hasn't licked stamps isn't fit to write letters. Naturally, that's when knowing whether the pie comes before the ice-cream, and how to drive a motor car, won't be a scrap of real use to you.

I only mention these things cos I'm afraid your ideas about the footing you're coming into the house on have got a bit puffed up over in the East. I can give you a start, but after that you'll have to blast your own way to the front. It's all up to the man. If you gave some blokes a talent wrapped in a napkin to start out in business with, they'd swap the talent for a gold brick and lose the napkin; and there are others you could start off with just a napkin, who'd set up with it in the drapery business in a small way, and then coax the other bloke's talent into it.

I've got pride enough to reckon you've got the right sort of stuff in you, but I want to see some of it come out. You'll never make a good merchant of yourself by turning round the order the Lord laid down for us: learning the spending end of business before the earning end. Pay day's always a month off for the spendthrift, and he never manages to get more than sixty cents out of any dollar that comes his way. But a dollar's worth one hundred and six cents to a good businessman, and he never spends the dollar. It's the bloke who keeps his savings up and his expenses down who buys a share in the concern. That's where you're going to find yourself weak, if your expense accounts don't tell porkies; and they don't generally lie in that particular way, though Baron Munchausen was the first travelling salesman, and my drummers' bills still show his influence.
